claim: In green algae, a chlorophyll and carotenoid-binding protein, light-harvesting complex stress-related (LHCSR3), detects excess energy via a pH drop and serves as a quenching site.
source: In green algae, a chlorophyll and carotenoid-binding protein, light-harvesting complex stress-related (LHCSR3), detects excess energy via a pH drop and serves as a quenching site.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing established understanding about LHCSR3 function, supported by the experimental work in the manuscript.

claim: Two distinct quenching processes, individually controlled by pH and zeaxanthin, were identified within LHCSR3 in vitro.
source: In vitro two distinct quenching processes, individually controlled by pH and zeaxanthin, were identified within LHCSR3.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The pH-dependent quenching was removed within a mutant LHCSR3 that lacks the residues that are protonated to sense the pH drop.
source: The pH-dependent quenching was removed within a mutant LHCSR3 that lacks the residues that are protonated to sense the pH drop.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on stop-LHCSR3 mutant shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2G.

claim: Observation of quenching in zeaxanthin-enriched LHCSR3 even at neutral pH demonstrated zeaxanthin-dependent quenching.
source: Observation of quenching in zeaxanthin-enriched LHCSR3 even at neutral pH demonstrated zeaxanthin-dependent quenching, which also occurs in other light-harvesting complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by single-molecule data in Figure 1D and Figure 2.

claim: Either pH- or zeaxanthin-dependent quenching prevented the formation of damaging reactive oxygen species.
source: Either pH- or zeaxanthin-dependent quenching prevented the formation of damaging reactive oxygen species, and thus the two quenching processes may together provide different induction and recovery kinetics for photoprotection in a changing environment.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by SOSG measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: If NPQ were optimized for biomass, yields would improve dramatically, potentially by up to 30%.
source: If NPQ were optimized for biomass, yields would improve dramatically, potentially by up to 30% (Kromdijk et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Kromdijk et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2010.

claim: In Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, LHCSR is the key gene product for NPQ.
source: In Chlamydomonas (C.) reinhardtii, the model organism for green algae, light-harvesting complex stress-related (LHCSR) is the key gene product for NPQ.
evidence: This is an established fact about C. reinhardtii supported by scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Two isoforms of LHCSR, LHCSR1 and LHCSR3, are active in NPQ, although LHCSR3 is accumulated at higher levels and so has the major role.
source: Two isoforms of LHCSR, LHCSR1 and LHCSR3, are active in NPQ, although LHCSR3 is accumulated at higher levels and so has the major role (Dinc et al., 2016; Maruyama et al., 2014; Peers et al., 2009; Tokutsu and Minagawa, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The primary proposals for the photophysical mechanism of quenching in light-harvesting complexes involve Chl-Car interactions.
source: While the photophysical mechanism of quenching in light-harvesting complexes has not been determined, the primary proposals involve Chl-Car interactions (Liao et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2003; Ruban et al., 2007; Son et al., 2020a; Son et al., 2020b; de la Cruz Valbuena et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: NPQ is triggered by a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane that forms through a drop in luminal pH.
source: NPQ is triggered by a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane that forms through a drop in luminal pH (Horton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an established mechanism supported by citation to Horton et al., 1996.

claim: Lumen acidification generally occurs when the light available causes an imbalance between the proton generation and the capacity of the photosynthetic apparatus to use protons for ATP production.
source: Lumen acidification generally occurs when the light available causes an imbalance between the proton generation and the capacity of the photosynthetic apparatus to use protons for ATP production (Joliot and Finazzi, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joliot and Finazzi, 2010.

claim: The C-terminus of LHCSR3 contains a number of luminal residues that are protonated upon the pH drop to trigger quenching.
source: The C-terminus of LHCSR3 contains a number of luminal residues that are protonated upon the pH drop to trigger quenching (Ballottari et al., 2016; Liguori et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Ballottari et al., 2016 and Liguori et al., 2013.

claim: The pH drop activates the enzymatic conversion of the carotenoid violaxanthin to zeaxanthin.
source: The pH drop also activates the enzymatic conversion of the Car violaxanthin (Vio) to zeaxanthin (Zea) (Eskling et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eskling et al., 1997.

claim: In C. reinhardtii, the CP26 and CP29 subunits have been implicated in NPQ.
source: In C. reinhardtii, the CP26 and CP29 subunits, which are minor antenna complexes of Photosystem II (PSII), have been implicated in NPQ (Cazzaniga et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cazzaniga et al., 2020.

claim: In higher plants, Zea has been reported to be involved in NPQ induction by driving light-harvesting complexes into a quenched state and/or by mediating interaction between light-harvesting complexes and PsbS.
source: In higher plants, Zea has been reported to be involved in NPQ induction by driving light-harvesting complexes into a quenched state and/or by mediating interaction between light-harvesting complexes and PsbS, nonpigment binding subunits essential for NPQ induction in vascular plants (Sacharz et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2008; Jahns and Holzwarth, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sacharz et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2008; and Jahns and Holzwarth, 2012.

claim: Zea binding to LHCSR1 in the moss Physcomitrella patens and LHCX1 in the microalga Nannochloropsis oceanica has been shown to be essential for NPQ.
source: Similarly, Zea binding to LHCSR1 in the moss Physcomitrella patens and LHCX1 (a LHCSR homolog) in the microalga Nannochloropsis oceanica has been shown to be essential for NPQ (Pinnola et al., 2013; Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pinnola et al., 2013 and Park et al., 2019.

claim: In C. reinhardtii, a reduction of NPQ in the absence of Zea has been reported.
source: Finally, in C. reinhardtii, a reduction of NPQ in the absence of Zea has been reported (Niyogi et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Niyogi et al., 1997.

claim: Recent work has shown Zea to be unnecessary for NPQ induction or related to highly specific growth conditions.
source: In contrast, recent work has shown Zea to be unnecessary for NPQ induction or related to highly specific growth conditions (Bonente et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2019; Vidal-Meireles et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonente et al., 2011; Tian et al., 2019; and Vidal-Meireles et al., 2020.

claim: The contribution of Zea to quenching in green algae remains under debate.
source: Thus, the contribution of Zea to quenching in green algae remains under debate.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the conflicting findings cited in the previous sentences.

claim: In the WT strains, the maximum NPQ level was reached after 10 min of illumination and fully recovered in the dark.
source: In the WT strains, the maximum NPQ level was reached after 10 min of illumination and fully recovered in the dark (Figure 1A, black), despite a strong accumulation of Zea (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The recovery of the NPQ traces to similar levels for all mutants acclimated to HL demonstrated that the photodamage was limited, if any, for these cells during the 60 min of illumination.
source: The recovery of the NPQ traces to similar levels for all mutants acclimated to HL demonstrated that the photodamage, known as photoinhibition, was limited, if any, for these cells during the 60 min of illumination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NPQ recovery data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The major component of NPQ in C. reinhardtii is Zea-independent.
source: The low level of these two processes observed in our NPQ measurements also suggests that the major component of NPQ in C.reinhardtii is Zea-independent, in agreement with previous results (Bonente et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the NPQ data and citation to Bonente et al., 2011.

claim: In the npq4 lhcsr1 strain, which lacks LHCSR subunits, a null NPQ phenotype was observed in both HL and LL acclimated cells.
source: In the npq4 lhcsr1 strain, which lacks LHCSR subunits, a null NPQ phenotype was observed in both HL and LL acclimated cells (Figure 1A, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LHCSR subunits are responsible for light-dependent NPQ in C. reinhardtii.
source: These results confirm that LHCSR subunits are responsible for light-dependent NPQ in C. reinhardtii as previously reported (Peers et al., 2009; Ballottari et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the NPQ data from the npq4 lhcsr1 mutant and citations to previous work.

claim: Upon a decrease in pH from 7.5 to 5.0, the median fluorescence intensity of LHCSR3-Vio decreased by ~5 counts/10 ms due to an increase in the quenched population.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, upon a decrease in pH from 7.5 to 5.0, the median fluorescence intensity of LHCSR3-Vio decreased by ~5 counts/10 ms due to an increase in the quenched population, reflecting additional quenching of the excitation energy absorbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule fluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Stop-LHCSR3 with Vio exhibited similar fluorescence intensity at pH 7.5 and pH 5.0, where the median intensity even increases at low pH.
source: Upon the same pH decrease that induced quenching in LHCSR3-Vio, stop-LHCSR3 with Vio (stop-LHCSR3-Vio) exhibited similar fluorescence intensity where the median intensity even increases, primarily due to increased heterogeneity in the fluorescence emission at low pH as seen through the standard deviation of the two distributions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule fluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The stop-LHCSR3 mutants have lost the ability to activate quenching channels upon a pH drop.
source: The data show that the mutants have lost the ability to activate quenching channels upon a pH drop, highlighting the sensing role of the residues of the C-terminus of LHCSR3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single-molecule data on stop-LHCSR3 shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LHCSR3-Zea in vitro showed a decrease in median fluorescence intensity by ~10–12 counts/10 ms compared to LHCSR3-Vio under both pH 7.5 and pH 5.0 conditions.
source: Under both conditions, as shown in Figure 1D, LHCSR3-Zea in vitro showed a decrease in median fluorescence intensity by ~10–12 counts/10 ms compared to LHCSR3-Vio.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule fluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The pH-independence of LHCSR3-Zea fluorescence histograms is consistent with the in vivo NPQ measurements in the zep mutants where HL does not change quenching levels.
source: The pH-independence of these histograms is consistent with the in vivo NPQ measurements in the zep mutants where HL, and the associated pH drop in the lumen, does not change quenching levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting in vitro single-molecule data with in vivo NPQ measurements.

claim: Two lifetime states were observed in the distributions for each of the LHCSR3 samples: an unquenched state (~2.5 ns) and a quenched state (~0.5 ns).
source: For each of the LHCSR3 samples, two lifetime states were observed in the distributions, an unquenched state (~2.5 ns) and a quenched state (~0.5 ns).
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Three dynamic components were identified within single LHCSR3, indicating multiple Chl a emissive sites within each LHCSR3.
source: Because three components were observed within single LHCSR3, they indicate multiple Chl a emissive sites within each LHCSR3, consistent with previous models of LHCs (Mascoli et al., 2019; Mascoli et al., 2020; Krüger et al., 2010; Krüger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis and citations to previous work on LHCs.

claim: In LHCSR3-Vio, a decrease in pH from 7.5 to 5.0 stabilizes the quenched state by decreasing the transition rate from the quenched to the unquenched state.
source: In LHCSR3-Vio, the quenched state is stabilized by a decrease in the transition rate from the quenched to the unquenched state, corresponding to a higher barrier in the free-energy landscape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In stop-LHCSR3-Vio, no change in the population of the quenched state is observed upon a decrease in pH.
source: In stop-LHCSR3-Vio, however, no change in the population of the quenched state is observed upon a decrease in pH (Figure 2G), reflecting the expected pH-independence of the sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: At both pH 7.5 and pH 5.0, conversion from Vio to Zea stabilizes the quenched state via a decrease in the transition rate from the quenched to unquenched state.
source: At both pH levels, conversion from Vio to Zea stabilizes the quenched state via a decrease in the transition rate from the quenched to unquenched state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The Zea-dependent behavior is maintained for stop-LHCSR3, where the quenched state is still stabilized in the presence of Zea.
source: The Zea-dependent behavior is maintained for stop-LHCSR3 (Figure 2K), where the quenched state is still stabilized in the presence of Zea.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: WT cells and npq1 cells acclimated to HL show a faster fluorescence decay after exposure to 60 min of HL.
source: WT cells and npq1 cells, which lack Zea, acclimated to HL show a faster fluorescence decay, or an increase in quenching, after exposure to 60 min of HL (Figure 3A, gray bars, fluorescence decays and fits to data shown in SI).
evidence: This claim is supported by 77K fluorescence lifetime measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For npq4 lhcsr1 cells, which lack LHCSR, similar fluorescence decay kinetics were measured regardless of light treatment.
source: For npq4 lhcsr1 cells, which lack LHCSR, similar fluorescence decay kinetics were measured regardless of light treatment (Figure 3A, purple), which is comparable to the unquenched kinetics of WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by 77K fluorescence lifetime measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The npq1 strain shows that quenching can occur without Zea, that is, induced by the pH drop alone.
source: While the results from WT show a role for pH and/or Zea in light-induced quenching in LHCSR3, the results from the npq1 strain show that quenching can occur without Zea, that is, induced by the pH drop alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 77K fluorescence lifetime data from the npq1 strain.

claim: The zep mutant presented a faster fluorescence decay among all samples, regardless of HL or LL acclimation or light treatment, compared to the decay of dark-adapted WT.
source: The zep mutant, which constitutively accumulates Zea, presented a similar decay among all samples, regardless of HL or LL acclimation or light treatment, that was much faster, or more quenched, compared to the decay of dark-adapted WT (Figure 3A, red, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by 77K fluorescence lifetime measurements shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: The quenching observed in the zep mutant is consistent with the pH-independent quenching observed through the single-molecule fluorescence.
source: These results indicate quenching upon Zea accumulation alone, consistent with the reduced Fv/Fm observed in this mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 7). This result is also consistent with the pH-independent quenching observed through the single-molecule fluorescence shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2E and F.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting in vivo fluorescence lifetime data with single-molecule data.

claim: Light-harvesting complexes isolated from the zep mutant had a twofold higher content of Zea compared to the same fraction isolated from WT under the same conditions.
source: These complexes had a twofold higher content of Zea compared to the same fraction isolated from WT (CC4349) under the same conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by pigment analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The light-harvesting complexes isolated from the zep mutant showed a 10% decrease in the fluorescence lifetime.
source: The light-harvesting complexes isolated from the zep mutant also showed a 10% decrease in the fluorescence lifetime, suggesting that Zea-dependent quenching is at least somewhat shared with other light-harvesting complexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 5—source data 1, and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence lifetime measurements on isolated complexes.

claim: No major differences in quenching properties were found in monomeric and trimeric LHC complexes isolated from WT cells before or after exposure to 60 min of HL.
source: In contrast, no major differences in quenching properties were found in monomeric and trimeric LHC complexes isolated from WT cells before or after exposure to 60 min of HL, consistent with previous findings from higher plants and other green algae (Xu et al., 2015; Girolomoni et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence lifetime measurements and citations to previous work.

claim: The npq4 lhcsr1 strain demonstrated the highest level of singlet oxygen production, regardless of light treatment.
source: As expected from the low level of NPQ induction, npq4 lhcsr1, which lacks LHCSR, demonstrated the highest level of singlet oxygen production, regardless of light treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by SOSG measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The effect of Zea on singlet oxygen production was almost negligible in HL acclimated samples.
source: Interestingly, the effect of Zea was almost negligible in HL acclimated samples (with a very high NPQ induction).
evidence: This claim is supported by SOSG measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amount of singlet oxygen production was correlated with average lifetime, that is, inversely correlated with quenching.
source: Notably, the amount of singlet oxygen production was correlated with average lifetime (Figure 3A), that is, inversely correlated with quenching, confirming that the quenching of Chl singlet excited states investigated here plays a role in photoprotection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between SOSG and fluorescence lifetime data.

claim: Two dynamic components were identified through the 2D-FLC analysis that suggest two distinct photoprotective processes, one pH-dependent and one Zea-dependent, operating simultaneously within LHCSR3.
source: Two dynamic components were identified through the 2D-FLC analysis that suggest two distinct photoprotective processes, one pH-dependent and one Zea-dependent, operating simultaneously within LHCSR3.
evidence: This is a summary of the 2D-FLC analysis results presented in Figure 2.

claim: Each dynamic component likely arises from a Chl-Car pair, where the Car can quench the emissive Chl.
source: Each component likely arises from a Chl-Car pair, where the Car can quench the emissive Chl.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 2D-FLC analysis results based on structural considerations.

claim: The pH-dependent component likely involves Lut and the neighboring Chl a 613.
source: The pH-dependent component (Figure 2E–H) likely involves Lut and the neighboring Chl a 613.
evidence: This is a structural assignment based on the 2D-FLC analysis and previous spectroscopic work.

claim: The Zea-dependent component likely involves Vio/Zea and the neighboring Chl as 602–603.
source: The Zea-dependent component (Figure 2J–K) likely involves Vio/Zea and the neighboring Chl as 602–603 (Bonente et al., 2011; Di Valentin et al., 2009; Lampoura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a structural assignment based on the 2D-FLC analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: With a decrease in pH from 7.5 to 5.0, the equilibrium free-energy differences for the pH-dependent component were shifted toward the quenched state by over 200 cm−1 in LHCSR3-Vio and over 500 cm−1 in LHCSR3-Zea.
source: With a decrease in pH from 7.5 to 5.0, the equilibrium free-energy differences for the pH-dependent component, which were calculated using the relative rate constants from the global fit, were shifted toward the quenched state by over 200 cm−1 in LHCSR3-Vio and over 500 cm−1 in LHCSR3-Zea (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis and free-energy calculations.

claim: The negligible change in the equilibrium free-energy difference for stop-LHCSR3 upon a pH drop demonstrates the functional role of the C-terminal tail in the conformational change into the quenched state.
source: The negligible (<30 cm−1) change in the equilibrium free-energy difference for this mutant (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 1) upon a pH drop demonstrates the functional role of the C-terminal tail in the conformational change into the quenched state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 2D-FLC analysis on stop-LHCSR3.

claim: Upon substitution of Zea for Vio, the equilibrium free-energy difference becomes further biased toward the quenched state by over 550 cm−1 at pH 7.5 and over 300 cm−1 at pH 5.0.
source: Upon substitution of Zea for Vio, the equilibrium free-energy difference becomes further biased toward the quenched state by over 550 cm−1 at pH 7.5 and over 300 cm−1 at pH 5.0, where the difference was calculated from the populations of the lifetime states determined within the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis and free-energy calculations.

claim: In vivo full light-induced quenching upon lumen acidification was observed in the npq1 strain, which lacks Zea.
source: Likewise, in vivo full light-induced quenching upon lumen acidification was observed in the npq1 strain, which lacks Zea, and full quenching even at neutral pH was observed in the zep strain, which is Zea-enriched, suggesting two quenching and induction processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo NPQ and fluorescence lifetime measurements.

claim: Full quenching even at neutral pH was observed in the zep strain, which is Zea-enriched.
source: Likewise, in vivo full light-induced quenching upon lumen acidification was observed in the npq1 strain, which lacks Zea, and full quenching even at neutral pH was observed in the zep strain, which is Zea-enriched, suggesting two quenching and induction processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo NPQ and fluorescence lifetime measurements.

claim: The 2D-FLC analysis of the stop-LHCSR3 mutant shows that removal of the C-terminal tail removes pH-dependent quenching, while leaving Zea-dependent quenching nearly unaffected.
source: The 2D-FLC analysis of the stop-LHCSR3 mutant shows that removal of the C-terminal tail removes pH-dependent quenching, while leaving Zea-dependent quenching nearly unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 2D-FLC analysis on stop-LHCSR3 shown in Figure 2.

claim: The in vivo and in vitro results indicated that either pH- or Zea-dependent quenching provides efficient photoprotection.
source: Taken together, the in vivo and in vitro results indicated that either pH- or Zea-dependent quenching provides efficient photoprotection.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the combined in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: pH- and Zea-dependent quenching may both contribute to all quenching in the WT, while being alternatively triggered in the mutants through a compensatory effect.
source: Thus, pH- and Zea-dependent quenching may both contribute to all quenching in the WT, while being alternatively triggered in the mutants through a compensatory effect.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results considering potential compensatory mechanisms.

claim: The two quenching processes act in combination to provide different time scales of activation and deactivation of photoprotection, allowing survival under variable light conditions.
source: The two quenching processes act in combination to provide different time scales of activation and deactivation of photoprotection, allowing survival under variable light conditions.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the two distinct quenching processes identified.

claim: LHCSR3 contains eight Chl molecules (7–8 Chl a and 0–1 Chl b molecules) and two Cars (one lutein and one Vio or Zea).
source: As shown in Figure 2—source data 2, LHCSR3 purified from C. reinhardtii contains eight Chl molecules (7–8 Chl a and 0–1 Chl b molecules) and two Cars (one lutein [Lut] and one Vio or Zea).
evidence: This claim is supported by pigment composition data shown in Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: Zea-dependent quenching is observed both in vivo and in vitro even at neutral pH.
source: Zea-dependent quenching is observed both in vivo and in vitro even at neutral pH.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claim: A strong reduction of fluorescence lifetime was observed in whole cells in the case of zep mutant, even in LL acclimated cells where the amount of LHCSR3 is minimal.
source: A strong reduction of fluorescence lifetime was observed in whole cells in the case of zep mutant, even in LL acclimated cells where the amount of LHCSR3 is minimal (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence lifetime measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: LHCSR subunits are not the sole quenching site where Zea-dependent quenching occurs.
source: This indicated that LHCSR subunits are not the sole quenching site where Zea-dependent quenching occurs, as seen in previous work implicating the minor antenna complexes (Cazzaniga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the zep mutant data and citation to previous work.

claim: Zea-dependent quenching was measured in other light-harvesting complexes isolated from the zep mutant, but it was not sufficient to fully explain the strong quenching observed in whole cells.
source: Consistently, Zea-dependent quenching was measured in other light-harvesting complexes isolated from the zep mutant, but it was not sufficient to fully explain the strong quenching observed in whole cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the isolated complex data compared to whole cell measurements.

claim: In the case of the zep mutant, not only does Zea completely substitute Vio, but also the Zea/Chl ratio is much higher (~10 fold) compared to the ratio observed in WT or npq4 lhcsr1.
source: In the case of the zep mutant, not only does Zea completely substitute Vio (de-epoxidation index is 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but also the Zea/Chl ratio is much higher (~10 fold) compared to the ratio observed in WT or npq4 lhcsr1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pigment analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The strong quenching observed in the zep mutant could be related to accumulation of Zea in the thylakoid membrane changing the environment where the photosystems and light-harvesting complexes are embedded.
source: This suggests an alternative possibility where the strong quenching observed in the zep mutant could be related to accumulation of Zea in the thylakoid membrane changing the environment where the photosystems and light-harvesting complexes are embedded, inducing the latter to a strong quenched state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the zep mutant phenotype.

claim: Zea has been previously reported to influence the assembly and organization of light-harvesting complexes in the thylakoid membranes of higher plants, affecting their quenching properties.
source: Indeed, Zea has been previously reported to influence the assembly and organization of light-harvesting complexes in the thylakoid membranes of higher plants, affecting their quenching properties (Sacharz et al., 2017, Shukla et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sacharz et al., 2017 and Shukla et al., 2020.

claim: The pH-independent quenching in the presence of Zea is potentially the origin of the seemingly conflicting results in the literature regarding Zea's role in NPQ.
source: While both possibilities allow for quenching in the presence of Zea even at neutral pH, it is the pH-independent quenching itself that is potentially the origin of the seemingly conflicting results in the literature, where Zea has been found to both reduce NPQ (Niyogi et al., 1997) and be unnecessary for its induction (Bonente et al., 2011; Baek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous conflicting literature.

claim: In vivo results point to pH and Zea controlling separate quenching processes within LHCSR3 and that either parameter can provide efficient induction of LHCSR3 to a quenched state for photoprotection.
source: Our in vitro results point to pH and Zea controlling separate quenching processes within LHCSR3 and that either parameter can provide efficient induction of LHCSR3 to a quenched state for photoprotection.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vitro findings from the 2D-FLC analysis.

claim: The 2D-FLC analysis on single LHCSR3 quantified two parallel dynamic components, or distinct quenching processes, one of which is pH-dependent and the other Zea-dependent.
source: The 2D-FLC analysis on single LHCSR3 quantified two parallel dynamic components, or distinct quenching processes, one of which is pH-dependent and the other Zea-dependent.
evidence: This is a summary of the 2D-FLC analysis results.

claim: In vivo full light-induced quenching upon lumen acidification was observed in the npq1 strain, which lacks Zea, suggesting two quenching and induction processes.
source: Likewise, in vivo full light-induced quenching upon lumen acidification was observed in the npq1 strain, which lacks Zea, and full quenching even at neutral pH was observed in the zep strain, which is Zea-enriched, suggesting two quenching and induction processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the in vivo NPQ and fluorescence lifetime data.

claim: The WT LL grown strains, with reduced LHCSR accumulation, present a significantly lower NPQ induction, supporting the critical role of the protonation of the C terminus residues unique to LHCSR in activating quenching in C. reinhardtii.
source: Analogously, the WT LL grown strains, with reduced LHCSR accumulation, also present a significantly lower NPQ induction, supporting the critical role of the protonation of the C terminus residues unique to LHCSR in activating quenching in C. reinhardtii.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NPQ data from LL-grown strains.

claim: While in vivo measurements suggest that pH-dependent quenching is often dominant over Zea-dependent quenching, the conformational states and pigment pairs likely responsible exhibit spectroscopic signatures that suggest both quenching processes have similar conformational dynamics.
source: While in vivo measurements suggest that pH-dependent quenching is often dominant over Zea-dependent quenching, and correspondingly more efficient in photoprotection, the conformational states and pigment pairs likely responsible exhibit spectroscopic signatures that suggest both quenching processes have similar conformational dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: pH- and Zea-dependent quenching may both contribute to all quenching in the WT, while being alternatively triggered in the mutants through a compensatory effect.
source: Thus, pH- and Zea-dependent quenching may both contribute to all quenching in the WT, while being alternatively triggered in the mutants through a compensatory effect.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation considering potential compensatory mechanisms in mutants.

claim: Under natural conditions, pH- and Zea-dependent quenching processes combine to protect the system and there is likely interplay between them through compensatory acclimation or changes to the protein organization within the thylakoid.
source: Under natural conditions, these processes combine to protect the system and there is likely interplay between them through compensatory acclimation or changes to the protein organization within the thylakoid.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about how the two processes work together in nature.
